title: A Program That Asks: Reading a Number a Person Typed, and the Four Ways It Goes Wrong

questions.question: A person types 12abc and the program reads it with in >> value. What happens?
options: It succeeds with 12 and leaves abc in the stream, so a mistake is accepted without a word
questions.explanation: The suite prints 12abc, 3,5, 7 8 and 9.5.1 read as 12, 3, 7 and 9.5.

questions.question: After a failed read, why do later reads fail even when the person types good numbers?
options: The stream is in a failed state until cleared, and the bad text is still in it
questions.explanation: Ten reads of abc then three sevens with no clean up: 0 succeeded.

questions.question: What two lines clean up after a failed read?
options: in.clear() for the failed state and in.ignore(..., '\n') for the bad line
questions.explanation: In that order: clearing first, then discarding the line.

questions.question: Why is 400 for a limit of 100 reported differently from abc?
options: It is a valid number that is no use as an answer, and a person needs to be told which of the two it was
questions.explanation: The limits themselves, 0 and 100, are accepted.

questions.question: A script runs a program that asks until satisfied, and the input file ends. What happens with no bound and no end of input check?
options: Every read fails, the loop answers by asking again, and the program hangs, though it works when tried by hand
questions.explanation: Asking an empty input up to 1000 times used 1 attempt, because ask stops at the end of the input.

questions.question: Why do the tests feed the functions from text in memory?
options: Nothing waits for a keyboard, so the suite runs in a script and always finishes; the same trick tests anything that asks
questions.explanation: A test that needs a person at a keyboard cannot run on a build server.
